nameStory: The Peach Root Weevil gets its name from its love affair with peach tree roots, where both adults and larvae cause damage by feeding and boring tunnels. Despite the specific name, this little beetle isn't picky—it will also attack other stone fruit trees like plums and cherries when peaches aren't available.
description: The Peach Root Weevil is a small, dark beetle that belongs to the broad-nosed weevil family. Like all weevils, it has a distinctive snout (called a rostrum) that it uses for drilling into plant material. These compact beetles are typically dark brown to black and have the characteristic stocky build of broad-nosed weevils. Originally from Japan, this species has established itself in eastern North America where it's become a familiar sight around stone fruit trees.

idTips.label: Broad snout
idTips.description: The short, wide rostrum (snout) is much broader than it is long, giving the head a flattened appearance when viewed from above

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Body is uniformly dark brown to black with a somewhat matte finish, lacking any bright metallic sheen

idTips.label: Compact size
idTips.description: Small beetles that feel solid and weighty for their size when gently handled, with a distinctly oval profile

idTips.label: Elbow-shaped antennae
idTips.description: Antennae have a distinct bend (elbow) in the middle and end in a small club, typical of weevil family members

idTips.label: Textured wing covers
idTips.description: Wing covers have faint rows of tiny punctures that create subtle ridges you can feel with a fingertip

habitat: Look for Peach Root Weevils in orchards, gardens, and anywhere stone fruit trees grow throughout New England. They're particularly common around peach, plum, and cherry trees, both cultivated varieties and wild specimens. Adults often hide in soil or leaf litter near the base of host trees during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering sites and become active, beginning to feed on tree bark and lay eggs near root systems of host plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible feeding on bark and moving between trees. Look for small notches chewed in bark around the base of stone fruit trees.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding to build up energy reserves before winter, making this another good time to spot them active on warm days.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in soil, leaf litter, or other protected spots near host trees, remaining inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This international traveler made an 8,000-mile journey from Japan to establish itself in North America, likely hitchhiking in plant material or soil, proving that even tiny beetles can become successful globetrotters!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small dark weevils, but the Peach Root Weevil's distinctly broad snout sets it apart—if the snout looks almost as wide as it is long, you've found your weevil. Many other weevils have much longer, more needle-like snouts.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the "Peach" Root Weevil, this species readily attacks other stone fruits, so don't be surprised to find it on plum or cherry trees. The scientific name honors a researcher named Hiller, and the recent genus change in 2006 reflects ongoing research into weevil relationships.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Pseudoedophrys found in New England, the Peach Root Weevil is unique in combining its broad snout with its specific dark coloration and size. Other broad-nosed weevils in the area tend to be either much larger, have different color patterns, or possess distinctly longer snouts, making this species relatively easy to distinguish once you know what to look for.
